newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Europe coffee drinkers to pay more on supply fears.
newsitem.headline: Europe coffee drinkers to pay more on supply fears.

text.p: World prices for raw coffee have staged a blistering rally this year and consumers across Europe are now feeling the heat.

Fears over tight coffee supplies from key growers in Latin America and dangerously low consumer stocks have fuelled an explosive surge in world prices -- the New York market has more than doubled since late 1996.
On Wednesday, leading Dutch roaster Douwe Egberts became the latest to raise prices, pushing up the retail price for a standard pack in the Netherlands for the third time this year.

"The market is incredibly high and its no wonder the retailers are putting up prices. Roasters have been concerned about a shortage of washed arabica coffee," said Neil Rosser, coffee analyst at trade house E.D. and F. Man in London.

This latest Dutch increase takes the average price for 250 grammes of coffee to four guilders, more than 20 percent up on January's level. The company, part of the giant Sara Lee Corporation of the United States, said it had no option while faced with the state of the world market.
"It is Douwe Egberts policy to change the retail price in response to the higher structural price of green coffee on the world market," spokesman Joost den Haan told Reuters.
In Germany, the world's second biggest market, consumers are also paying more, although fierce competition there is so far keeping a lid on much of the increase.
"The problem is that earlier price increases have not fully reached the consumer," one coffee analyst commented.

Average retail prices have only risen by some seven percent since January but last Friday Germany's market leader Kraft Jacobs Suchard, part of Philip Morris, warned it would probably announce a price hike this week.
On Tuesday, Swiss coffee giant Nestle SA said it needed to raise its prices by between 10 and 15 percent.
Attention has been focused on the New York futures market, which trades the quality arabica beans grown in Latin America and used widely in premium coffees drunk in continental Europe.
The market in London, which trades the robusta variety used mostly in instant soluble coffees, has been less affected.

New York prices have shot up to levels not seen since the major Brazilian frost scare three years ago, more than doubling in around six months while those for London's robusta variety are up by about a third.
In New York trading on Tuesday, coffee for May delivery reached 263.40 cents a pound, within 10 cents of the level hit in July 1994, when frost badly damaged the Brazil crop.
Smaller-than-expected crops across Latin America, including the top two producers, Brazil and Colombia, are to blame.
Traders say the Colombian harvest this season could be below 10 million (60 kg) bags, compared to last season's 13 million.
And news this week the country's truck drivers could stage another nationwide strike heightened supply concerns, although that threat seems to have abated for now.
On Tuesday, German trading house Bernhard Rothfos put Brazil's 1997/98 crop at between 24 and 25.5 million bags, well down on the previous year's 30 million.
The trade is also aware that with the onset of the frost season in Brazil, further wild swings in prices are possible.

On Monday, news of a fire at a coffee warehouse in Costa Rica was enough to ignite the market. Although the amount destroyed was not great, the country produces the mild arabica variety most sought after by U.S. roasters.

The other factor has been largely of the roasters' own making, analysts say. Faced with a turbulent market, roasters have been buying only to cover immediate needs and this has allowed their stocks in the United States and Europe to dwindle.
"Stocks are low and it's because of the roasters' philosophy of buying just hand-to-mouth," one analyst said.
"If the market stays where it is, then another round of price rises in the shops looks inevitable," he added.
